## A short introduction 

Our goal here is to get a first draft of the *Crepidostomum sp* genome. 
To do this, we have different types of data that we have previously
processed:
   - Nanopore Minion. We have done the basecalling: Ex68_3
   - PacBio. Confused data: take a good look at it. According to Isa,
     she also got hold of two individuals of *Crepidostomum*, but they
     are not the same as those of Nanopore. And they are not parasites
     of *Coregonus*, but of Arctic charr.
   - Illumina Shot Gun. Two compressed FASTQ files for *Crepidostomum*.
     A single individual: Ex71_6.

As for mount options, I have mainly two:

1. Do two genome drafts: first with the Nanopore MinIon data and then
   with the PacBio data. In this way we could determine which are the
   data that present a better coverage and use them as a "base".
2. Make a single genome draft with all the data, without distinction by
   individual. This is made possible by flye's option to collapse the
   similar regions of haplotypes. Less optimal due to the loss of quality
   or accuracy of the genome draft.

So, first of all, `flye` is executed with the Nanopore and PacBio rawdata,
that is, to make a hybrid assembly of both types of long sequences. I will
take the PacBio data as base first, and next, Nanopore data as base.
Finally, a polish is done with the Illumina data.

# Assembly with FLYE
## Hybrid assembly with both PacBio and Nanopore 

Recall (`2023-04-19`) that PacBio dataset consists on 123310 reads of variable
length between 51 and 23873 bases, while Nanopore data includes 608000 reads with
between 9 and 97021 bases (before trimming). The read qualities are higher in the
the smaller, PacBio data set. Also recall the *k*-mer analysis on the Illumina
reads suggested a genome length in the order of 680 million base pairs with
high heterozygosity.

NOTE: flye: error: argument --pacbio-hifi: not allowed with argument --nano-hq
Flye does not acceot the two arguments in the same run. Lucky for us, the author
resolved this issue in his Github:
[https://github.com/fenderglass/Flye/issues/98](https://github.com/fenderglass/Flye/issues/98).
It is also currently documented [here](https://github.com/mikolmogorov/Flye/blob/flye/docs/FAQ.md#can-i-use-both-pacbio-and-ont-reads-for-assembly).

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
## Solution from the author in GitHub. Not run.

flye --pacbio-raw $PBREADS $ONTREADS \
     --iterations 0 --out-dir $OUTPUTDIR  \
     --genome-size 3.5g --threads $THREADS

flye --pacbio-raw $PBREADS \
     --resume-from polishing \
     --out-dir $OUTPUTDIR  \
     --genome-size 3.5g \
     --threads $THREADS
```

```{bash}
if [ ! -d flye ]; then mkdir flye; fi

NANO="../2023-04-19/nanopore_trimmed/*.fastq"
PACBIO="../../data/PacBio/fastqs/demultiplex.bc1018_BAK8B_OA--bc1018_BAK8B_OA.hifi_reads.fastq"

OUT="flye/PB_ONT"

if [ ! -e flye/PB_ONT/assembly.fasta ]; then
  flye --pacbio-raw $PACBIO $NANO -o $OUT -t 16 --iterations 0    >  flye/assemblies.log
  flye --pacbio-raw $PACBIO -o $OUT -t 16 --resume-from polishing >> flye/assemblies.log
fi

OUT1="flye/ONT_PB"

if [ ! -e flye/ONT_PB/assembly.fasta ]; then
  flye --nano-raw $NANO $PACBIO -o $OUT1 -t 16 --iterations 0     >> flye/assemblies.log
  flye --nano-raw $NANO -o $OUT1 -t 16 --resume-from polishing    >> flye/assemblies.log
fi
```

## Distribution of contig lengths

```{r contigLengths, eval=TRUE}
nanoAssembly <- read.table('flye/ONT_PB/assembly_info.txt',
                           col.names = c('contig', 'length', 'cov', 'circ',
                                         'repeat', 'mult', 'skip', 'skip'),
                           colClasses = c('character', 'numeric', 'numeric',
                                          'factor', 'factor', 'numeric',
                                          'NULL', 'NULL'))
pacbioAssembly <- read.table('flye/PB_ONT/assembly_info.txt',
                             col.names = c('contig', 'length', 'cov', 'circ',
                                           'repeat', 'mult', 'skip', 'skip'),
                             colClasses = c('character', 'numeric', 'numeric',
                                            'factor', 'factor', 'numeric',
                                            'NULL', 'NULL'))
stopifnot(! is.unsorted(rev(pacbioAssembly$length)))
stopifnot(! is.unsorted(rev(nanoAssembly$length)))
nanoAssembly$sum <- cumsum(nanoAssembly$length)
pacbioAssembly$sum <- cumsum(pacbioAssembly$length)
nanoSize <- sum(nanoAssembly$length)
pacbioSize <- sum(pacbioAssembly$length)
nanoN50  <- which(nanoAssembly$sum >= 0.5 * nanoSize)[1]
pacbioN50 <- which(pacbioAssembly$sum >= 0.5 * pacbioSize)[1]
#par(mar = c(7,4,4,1))
barplot(nanoAssembly$length, col = 'gray', border = 'gray',
        xlim = c(1,7000), ylim = c(0, 250000),
        xlab = '', ylab = 'Contig length (bp)', main = 'Ordered contigs')
abline(v = nanoN50, col = 'gray', lty = 2)
par(new = TRUE)
barplot(pacbioAssembly$length, col = 'black', axes = FALSE,
        xlim = c(1,7000), ylim = c(0, 250000),)
abline(v = pacbioN50, col = 'black', lty = 2)
#text(c(nanoN50, pacbioN50), c(150000, 150000), c('ONT_PB', 'PB_ONT'), srt = 90, pos = 4)
axis(1, at = c(nanoN50, pacbioN50), labels = c('ONT_PB\nN50', 'PB_ONT\nN50'), las = 2)
```

The decreasingly ordered lengths of contigs of both assemblies suggest that the
assembly made with Oxford Nanopore data (in gray above) is much better: contigs
and total assembly length are much longer than in the PacBio assembly.

## *Peaks* of coverage depth

```{r peakdepth, eval=TRUE}
plot(density(nanoAssembly$cov), xlim = c(0, 30), col = 'darkred',
     main = 'Density of mean coverage per contig',
     xlab = 'Mean coverage', ylab = 'Density')
lines(density(pacbioAssembly$cov), col = 'darkgreen')
legend('topright', col = c('darkred','darkgreen'), lty=1,
       legend = c('Oxford Nanopore', 'PacBio'))
```

Both assemblies show two peaks of coverage depth, at almost 5 and at almost 20.
Approximately 34% of contigs, but less than 15% of the assembly length, seem
to be represented over 4 times more than most of the genome. A factor of 4 in
coverage differences among genome portions suggests that the low-coverage
fraction is composed of allelic haplotypes that should be merged, while the
high-coverage fraction must be collapsed duplicated regions.
The *octoploid* fraction has a slightly higher GC content (not shown), possibly
indicating a different nature (just "repetitive") of those sequences. But, the
overlap in GC content distributions of the two genomic components is large. By
the way, @Petkeviciute2008 shows a species of *Crepidostomum* has 6 pairs of
chromosomes ($n=6$).

Contigs with a mean coverage higher than 25 should probably be excluded from
any analysis.

```{r removable, eval=TRUE}
write.table(nanoAssembly[nanoAssembly$cov > 25, 'contig'],
            file = 'overcovered_contigs.txt', row.names = FALSE,
            col.names = FALSE, quote=FALSE)
```


## Assess draft genome quality (BUSCO)

We are going to asses the quality of the draft genomes, first for 
`--pacbio-raw` option as base and the other for `--nano-raw` option
as base.

```{bash}
export PATH=$PATH:/opt/bbmap
BUSCOOUTPUT=flye/PB_ONT/busco/short_summary.specific.metazoa_odb10.busco.json
if [ ! -e $BUSCOOUTPUT ]; then
  busco -i flye/PB_ONT/assembly.fasta \
        -l metazoa_odb10 \
        --download_path busco \
        -o flye/PB_ONT/busco -m genome --cpu 16 \
        > flye/PB_ONT/busco.log
fi

BUSCOOUTPUT=flye/ONT_PB/busco/short_summary.specific.metazoa_odb10.busco.json
if [ ! -e $BUSCOOUTPUT ]; then
  busco -i flye/ONT_PB/assembly.fasta \
        -l metazoa_odb10 \
        --download_path busco \
        -o flye/ONT_PB/busco -m genome --cpu 16 \
        > flye/ONT_PB/busco.log
fi
```

```{r moreSummary, eval=TRUE}
library('jsonlite')
library('MetBrewer')
library('kableExtra')
nanoBusco <- 'flye/ONT_PB/busco/short_summary.specific.metazoa_odb10.busco.json'
pbioBusco <- 'flye/PB_ONT/busco/short_summary.specific.metazoa_odb10.busco.json'
  nano <- fromJSON(nanoBusco)
pacbio <- fromJSON(pbioBusco)
busco  <- as.matrix(data.frame(
  OxfordNanopore = c(nano$results$Missing,
                     nano$results$Fragmented,
                     nano$results$'Multi copy',
                     nano$results$'Single copy'),
  PacBio = c(pacbio$results$Missing,
             pacbio$results$Fragmented,
             pacbio$results$'Multi copy',
             pacbio$results$'Single copy')
))
rownames(busco) <- c('Missing', 'Fragmented', 'Multi-copy', 'Single-copy')
pal <- met.brewer(name = 'Tam', n = 4, type = 'discrete')
barplot(busco, col = pal, border = pal)
legend('bottomright', fill = pal,
       legend = c('Missing', 'Fragmented', 'Multi-copy', 'Single-copy'))

summaryTable <- data.frame(
   Assembly = c('Nanopore', 'Pacbio'),
   Scaffolds = c(nano$results$`Number of scaffolds`,
                 pacbio$results$`Number of scaffolds`),
   Contigs = c(nano$results$`Number of contigs`,
               pacbio$results$`Number of contigs`),
   TotalLength = c(nano$results$`Total length`,
                   pacbio$results$`Total length`),
   ScaffoldN50 = c(nano$results$`Scaffold N50`,
                   pacbio$results$`Scaffold N50`)
)
kable(summaryTable) %>% kable_styling()
```

BUSCO results confirm that the assembly made with Oxford Nanopore data
first is a little better, in that at least a few of the expected genes were
detected, either as single-copy or fragmented.
